02 · Normalization, drift correction and protein roll-up¶

Question: Which normalization and protein roll-up remove the technical variation found in Notebook 01, without removing real biology? And how do we know?

Input: the outputs of Notebook 01, in data/processed/:

  • the filtered precursor table
  • the sample table with QC verdicts (205 runs after the 4 pre-registered exclusions)

Outputs:

  • a normalized precursor matrix and a protein matrix, saved to data/processed/ for Notebook 03
  • figures saved to figures/02_*.png

Approach:

  • Every candidate method is scored on the same scorecard.
  • Whenever a method is fitted on some runs, it is scored on runs it never saw, so that no method can win by fitting its own test data.
  • Methods are judged against objectives fixed in Notebook 01, before any method was tried.
§ Question
1 What exactly are we trying to achieve, and how will it be scored?
2 Which candidate normalizations are there, and what does each assume?
3 How do they score?
4 Why do QC-anchored corrections, including the authors', underperform on samples?
5 Decision, and what the chosen normalization does to drift, structure and the plate-3 wells
6 Which protein roll-up should turn precursors into proteins?
7 Is the biology still there after the full pipeline?
8 Do the conclusions survive a different protein-group filter?
9 What about missing values?
10 Summary and outputs

1. Objectives and scoring scheme¶

What Notebook 01 asked for, and one correction¶

Notebook 01 set these objectives before any method was tried:

  1. Lower within-matrix CVs. Plasma and serum wells are technical replicates of one material each, so their variation is purely technical.
  2. Remove the drift component, the principal component that tracks injection order.
  3. Keep the matrix component (plasma vs serum).
  4. Keep the fibrinogen difference between plasma and serum.
  5. Test whether the weak plate-3 wells are rescued.

Correction to objective 1. Notebook 01 proposed the pooled QC's short-term CV (about 7%) as the target for samples. That target is wrong for samples:

  • The QC is one digest injected repeatedly, so its CV contains only injection-to-injection (instrument) noise.
  • Every sample well was digested separately, so sample CVs also contain sample-preparation noise, which normalization cannot remove.
  • §4 estimates that floor. The objective becomes: lower sample CVs as far as technical correction allows, without removing biology.

How methods are scored, and why this way¶

  • Fit and score on different runs. QC-anchored methods are fitted on the even-numbered pooled-QC injections only (20 runs). QC precision is then scored on the odd-numbered QC injections (19 runs), which no method ever sees during fitting.
  • The primary metric is the plasma and serum CV, because these are the samples a real study cares about.
  • One candidate (M7) learns its correction from the samples themselves. It is scored by cross-fitting: the runs are split into two halves, and each half is corrected only with curves learned from the other half. No run ever helps correct itself, so its score cannot be flattered by over-fitting.
  • The scorecard (src/evaluate.py) is identical for every method:
Metric Objective Better is
Median CV in held-out QC, plasma, serum 1 lower
Residual drift: Spearman ρ of run-level signal vs injection order 2 closer to 0
Largest |ρ| between any of the top-5 PCs and injection order (a correction can also create small components that track run order) 2 lower
|r| between PC1 and matrix (plasma vs serum) 3 stays high
Fibrinogen-A log2 plasma/serum, precursor level 4 stays about 5–6
Plate-3 row H offset vs other serum wells 5 closer to 0
In [2]:
# Load Notebook 01 outputs and keep only the runs that passed QC
precursors = pd.read_parquet(PROCESSED / "01_precursors_filtered.parquet")
meta = pd.read_csv(PROCESSED / "01_sample_table_qc.csv", index_col=0)
meta = meta[~meta["exclude"]].sort_values("injection_order")
# Plates are labels, not numbers; the CSV round-trip turns 3 into 3.0, so convert back to "3"
meta["plate"] = pd.to_numeric(meta["plate"], errors="coerce").astype("Int64").astype("string")
runs = meta.index
injection = meta["injection_order"].astype(float)

# Precursor x run matrices on the log2 scale (normalization works on log ratios)
raw = np.log2(qc.to_matrix(precursors, value="Precursor.Quantity")[runs])
diann_norm = np.log2(qc.to_matrix(precursors, value="Precursor.Normalised")[runs])

# Per-precursor annotations used below
rt = precursors.groupby("Precursor.Id")["RT"].median().reindex(raw.index)
annot = precursors.drop_duplicates("Precursor.Id").set_index("Precursor.Id")[
    ["Protein.Group", "Genes", "Proteotypic"]].reindex(raw.index)
is_fga = annot["Genes"] == "FGA"                        # positive-control features

# Split the pooled QC: even injections fit QC-anchored corrections, odd ones are held out
qc_runs = meta.index[meta["sample_type"] == "tQC"]      # already in injection order
qc_fit, qc_test = qc_runs[0::2], qc_runs[1::2]
print(f"{raw.shape[0]:,} precursors x {raw.shape[1]} runs | "
      f"pooled QC: {len(qc_fit)} for fitting, {len(qc_test)} held out")

3,674 precursors x 205 runs | pooled QC: 20 for fitting, 19 held out

2. Candidate normalizations and their assumptions¶

A normalization is a claim about where unwanted variation comes from. Each candidate makes a different claim, and that claim is what decides whether it is valid here.

# Method Assumption Why consider it
M0 None (raw) — Baseline
M1 Global median Runs differ by one constant factor (the amount loaded) The most common default
M2 DIA-NN RT-dependent (Precursor.Normalised) Most precursors at a given RT are unchanged in any run Applied by the authors upstream; treated as an external reference
M3 Own RT-dependent LOWESS (normalize.rt_lowess_normalize) Same as M2 A transparent re-implementation we control; it should reproduce M2
M4 QC-anchored straight line per precursor (the authors' correction) Drift is linear in time; the QC drifts like the samples The published choice
M5 QC-anchored LOWESS per precursor, with an RT-bin fallback The QC drifts like the samples, in any shape Built to fix M4's linearity problem found in Notebook 01, §9b
M6 M5, then M3 Both Do the two corrections add up?
M7 M3, then a per-precursor LOWESS drift curve fitted on the samples (each sample group's median removed first) Run order is randomized with respect to biology Uses 166 sample runs as the anchor instead of 20 QC injections. Valid here because plates and sample types are interleaved across the sequence (Notebook 01, §3).

The smoothing spans of M5 and M7 are not free choices. Each is picked on runs that did not take part in fitting: held-out QC injections for M5, and the cross-fitted sample halves for M7.

In [3]:
# Choose the LOWESS span for M5 using held-out QC runs only (no peeking at samples).
# Each span is fitted on the even QC runs and scored on the odd ones.
span_rows = []
for frac in [0.3, 0.5, 0.8]:
    corrected, n_fallback = normalize.qc_lowess_correction(raw, injection, qc_fit, rt, frac=frac)
    span_rows.append({"LOWESS span": frac,
                      "held-out QC median CV %": qc.cv_percent(2 ** corrected[qc_test], 0.7).median()})
span_table = pd.DataFrame(span_rows).set_index("LOWESS span")
best_frac = span_table["held-out QC median CV %"].idxmin()
print(f"Chosen span: {best_frac}  |  precursors using the RT-bin fallback: {n_fallback}")
span_table

# Apply every candidate. Each line is one claim about where unwanted variation comes from.
candidates = {
    "M0 raw": raw,
    "M1 global median": normalize.median_normalize(raw),
    "M2 DIA-NN RT-dependent": diann_norm,
    "M3 RT-LOWESS (own)": normalize.rt_lowess_normalize(raw, rt, frac=0.3),
    "M4 QC linear (authors)": normalize.qc_linear_correction(raw, injection, qc_fit),
}
candidates["M5 QC LOWESS"], _ = normalize.qc_lowess_correction(raw, injection, qc_fit, rt, frac=best_frac)
candidates["M6 QC LOWESS + RT-LOWESS"] = normalize.rt_lowess_normalize(candidates["M5 QC LOWESS"], rt, frac=0.3)

# M7: after M3, remove each precursor's remaining trend over injection order, learned from the samples.
# Cross-fitted: alternate runs (in injection order) form two halves; each half is corrected by the other.
m3 = candidates["M3 RT-LOWESS (own)"]
folds = [runs[0::2], runs[1::2]]
groups = meta["sample_type"]

def m7_correct(matrix, fit_runs, frac):
    return normalize.sample_drift_correction(matrix, injection, groups, fit_runs=fit_runs, frac=frac)[0]

m7_span = {}
for frac in [0.3, 0.5, 0.8]:                       # choose the span on cross-fitted sample precision
    trial = normalize.cross_fit(lambda m, fit: m7_correct(m, fit, frac), m3, folds)
    m7_span[frac] = np.mean([qc.cv_percent(2 ** trial[meta.index[meta["sample_type"] == g]], 0.7).median()
                             for g in ["Plasma", "Serum"]])
m7_frac = min(m7_span, key=m7_span.get)
print("M7 span -> mean cross-fitted sample CV %:", {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in m7_span.items()}, "| chosen:", m7_frac)
candidates["M7 RT-LOWESS + sample drift (cross-fitted)"] = normalize.cross_fit(
    lambda m, fit: m7_correct(m, fit, m7_frac), m3, folds)

# Check that our RT-LOWESS reproduces DIA-NN's own normalization (they share an assumption)
both = candidates["M3 RT-LOWESS (own)"].stack().to_frame("own").join(diann_norm.stack().rename("diann")).dropna()
diff = (both["own"] - both["diann"]) - (both["own"] - both["diann"]).median()
print(f"M3 vs M2: Pearson r = {both.corr().iloc[0, 1]:.4f}; "
      f"median |difference| = {diff.abs().median():.3f} log2")

M7 span -> mean cross-fitted sample CV %: {0.3: np.float64(10.8), 0.5: np.float64(10.81), 0.8: np.float64(10.8)} | chosen: 0.3

M3 vs M2: Pearson r = 0.9998; median |difference| = 0.029 log2

Interpretation

  • Global median normalization (M1) is not enough. It halves the CVs, but a principal component still tracks injection order almost perfectly (|ρ| = 0.96). Drift depends on retention time (Notebook 01, §9b), and one scale factor per run cannot remove that.
  • RT-dependent normalization (M2/M3) does most of the work. Sample CVs fall from 23–24% to about 11.5%, and run-level signal no longer tracks injection order. Our implementation reproduces DIA-NN's almost exactly (r = 0.9998, median difference 0.03 log2), which validates both.
  • But M2/M3 leave a smaller drift component: one of the top PCs (PC3, about 5% of variance) still tracks injection order at |ρ| = 0.94. Precursors at the same retention time drift at different rates, and a per-run curve over RT cannot capture precursor-specific trends.
  • QC-anchored corrections (M4, M5) win on held-out QC precision but lose on samples (13–15% CV), and leave drift components (|ρ| 0.79–0.84).
    • The authors' linear version (M4) is the weakest, as the non-linear drift predicted.
    • M6 (QC, then RT) improves the CVs, but one of its top PCs still tracks run order (|ρ| = 0.57), a sign of over-correction (§4).
  • M7 is the only method that removes every run-order component (max |ρ| = 0.09). It also has the lowest sample CVs (10.7% plasma, 10.9% serum), scored out-of-sample by cross-fitting.
    • Its smoothing span made no practical difference (10.80–10.81% across 0.3–0.8), so the result does not hinge on tuning.
  • No method removes biology: PC1 still separates plasma from serum (|r| = 0.99), and fibrinogen-A stays at 5.3–5.6 log2 everywhere.
  • Caveat: after M7, serum run-level signal keeps a weak positive trend (ρ = 0.18; with 75 runs, p ≈ 0.1, not significant).

4. Why do QC-anchored corrections underperform on the samples?¶

There are three hypotheses, each testable:

  1. The QC does not drift like the samples. A pooled QC re-injected over days can change in ways the samples do not, for example through adsorption or evaporation in its vial.
  2. Part of the data has no QC anchor. Precursors absent from the serum QC pool, such as plasma-only peptides, have to borrow a correction.
  3. Samples carry variation that drift correction cannot reach. Each well was digested separately, so well-to-well preparation differences stay after any drift correction.
In [7]:
# Hypothesis 1: compare each precursor's drift slope in the QC with its slope in serum samples.
# Serum is used because the QC is a serum pool, so the same precursors are measured in both.
def slopes(matrix, cols, min_values=30):
    x = injection[cols].to_numpy()
    out = {}
    for pid, row in matrix[cols].iterrows():
        ok = row.notna().to_numpy()
        if ok.sum() >= min_values:
            out[pid] = np.polyfit(x[ok], row.to_numpy()[ok], 1)[0] * 100   # log2 per 100 injections
    return pd.Series(out)

serum_runs = meta.index[meta["sample_type"] == "Serum"]
drift_slopes = pd.DataFrame({"QC": slopes(raw, qc_runs, 30), "Serum": slopes(raw, serum_runs, 60)}).dropna()

# Slope of serum drift on QC drift, through the origin: 1 means "the QC drifts exactly like serum"
ratio = (drift_slopes["Serum"] * drift_slopes["QC"]).sum() / (drift_slopes["QC"] ** 2).sum()
r = drift_slopes.corr().iloc[0, 1]
print(f"{len(drift_slopes):,} precursors | serum drift = {ratio:.2f} x QC drift (through origin); "
      f"correlation of slopes r = {r:.2f}")
print(f"Median slope, log2 per 100 injections: QC {drift_slopes['QC'].median():.3f}, "
      f"serum {drift_slopes['Serum'].median():.3f}")

# Hypothesis 2: how many precursors had no QC anchor?
_, n_fallback = normalize.qc_lowess_correction(raw, injection, qc_fit, rt, frac=best_frac)
print(f"\nPrecursors without enough QC values (correction borrowed from their RT bin): "
      f"{n_fallback} of {raw.shape[0]:,} ({n_fallback / raw.shape[0]:.0%})")

# Hypothesis 3: estimate the preparation-noise floor from the best-normalized data.
# If variances add, CV_sample^2 = CV_injection^2 + CV_preparation^2 (approximately)
best = board.loc["M7 RT-LOWESS + sample drift (cross-fitted)"]
cv_inj = best["CV % QC (held out)"]
for g in ["Plasma", "Serum"]:
    cv_prep = np.sqrt(best[f"CV % {g}"] ** 2 - cv_inj ** 2)
    print(f"{g}: CV {best[f'CV % {g}']:.1f}% = injection {cv_inj:.1f}% + preparation ~{cv_prep:.1f}% (added in quadrature)")

2,700 precursors | serum drift = 0.83 x QC drift (through origin); correlation of slopes r = 0.93
Median slope, log2 per 100 injections: QC -0.227, serum -0.193

Precursors without enough QC values (correction borrowed from their RT bin): 668 of 3,674 (18%)
Plasma: CV 10.7% = injection 6.5% + preparation ~8.5% (added in quadrature)
Serum: CV 10.9% = injection 6.5% + preparation ~8.8% (added in quadrature)

Interpretation

  • Hypothesis 1 holds: the QC over-states the samples' drift.
    • Precursor by precursor, serum samples drift about 0.8 times as fast as the QC, even though the drift pattern is shared (slopes correlate well).
    • A QC-anchored correction therefore over-corrects the samples. That is why the samples show positive residual drift after M4 and M5 (ρ ≈ +0.1 to +0.35 in the scoreboard).
    • The likeliest reason is that the QC vial was re-injected about 40 times over days, accumulating changes the samples never saw.
  • Hypothesis 2 contributes: about 18% of precursors have no QC anchor and borrow an RT-bin average.
  • Hypothesis 3 sets the floor: even after the best correction (M7), sample CVs of about 10.8% decompose into roughly 6.5% injection noise and roughly 8.5–9% preparation noise. No normalization can remove the preparation part, because it is genuinely different in each well. Only better sample prep, or replicate digests, could.

What this means. A pooled QC is excellent for monitoring an instrument. Using it to correct samples assumes it ages like the samples, and here it does not. Two better anchors are available:

  • the bulk of each run's own precursors, which is what RT-dependent normalization uses
  • the samples themselves: there are 166 of them, they are the material being corrected, and their run order is randomized. That is what M7 adds.

5. Decision: RT-dependent normalization, then sample-anchored drift correction (M7)¶

Option For Against
M7 Lowest out-of-sample sample CVs; the only method leaving no PC tied to run order; anchored on 166 sample runs rather than 20 QC injections; no assumption about the shape of the time course Requires randomized run order (true here, verified in Notebook 01, §3) and known sample groups to centre on. Precursors with too few values keep only the M3 correction.
M3 alone Simplest; validated against DIA-NN Leaves a precursor-specific drift component (|ρ| = 0.94, about 5% of variance) that would confound any comparison correlated with run order
M6 Good CVs Relies on the QC tracking the samples, which §4 shows it does not; creates an over-correction component (|ρ| = 0.57)

Decision: M7.

  • When it must not be used: in a design where run order is not randomized (for example, all treated samples run after all controls), M7 would remove biology along with drift. The fallback is then M3, with the QC used for monitoring only. That rule carries forward to the degrader dataset.
  • Fitting vs scoring: for the exported data the drift curves are fitted on all runs. The scores above come from the cross-fitted version, which is the honest estimate of performance. The in-sample fit looks about 0.5 CV points better, which is exactly the optimism cross-fitting guards against.
In [9]:

# Plate 3: were the weak wells (Notebook 01, section 13) a loading problem that normalization fixes?
def plate3_check(m):
    log2_runs = m.dropna()
    level = log2_runs.median()
    r_ref = qc.correlation_to_reference(m, meta)            # r to own sample type's median profile
    row_h = meta.index[(meta["plate"] == "3") & (meta["well_row"] == "H")]
    other = meta.index[(meta["sample_type"] == "Serum") & ~meta.index.isin(row_h)]
    return {"offset vs other serum (log2)": level[row_h].median() - level[other].median(),
            "median r, row H": r_ref[row_h].median(), "median r, other serum": r_ref[other].median()}

check = pd.DataFrame({"raw": plate3_check(raw), "after M3": plate3_check(m3), "after M7 (chosen)": plate3_check(normalized)}).T
print(check.to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))     # 4 decimals: the r differences are small

                   offset vs other serum (log2)  median r, row H  median r, other serum
raw                                     -0.4131           0.9870                 0.9951
after M3                                -0.0143           0.9882                 0.9967
after M7 (chosen)                       -0.0037           0.9884                 0.9976

What remains of the row-H problem? The offset is gone, but their correlation to the serum profile stays lower than for other serum wells. Two questions follow: how many precursors still deviate, and how much does that cost in precision?

# Remaining row-H wells after normalization: how far do their precursors deviate from other serum wells?
row_h = meta.index[(meta["plate"] == "3") & (meta["well_row"] == "H")]
serum_other = serum_runs_all = meta.index[meta["sample_type"] == "Serum"]
serum_other = serum_other.difference(row_h)
deviation = normalized[row_h].median(axis=1) - normalized[serum_other].median(axis=1)
rho_rt = spearmanr(deviation, rt.reindex(deviation.index), nan_policy="omit")[0]
print(f"Row-H wells kept: {len(row_h)} | precursors deviating by > 0.5 log2: {(deviation.abs() > 0.5).mean():.1%} "
      f"| deviation vs RT: Spearman rho = {rho_rt:+.2f}")

# Precision cost of keeping them
cv_with = qc.cv_percent(2 ** normalized[serum_runs_all], 0.7).median()
cv_without = qc.cv_percent(2 ** normalized[serum_other], 0.7).median()
print(f"Serum precursor CV: {cv_with:.1f}% with row H, {cv_without:.1f}% without")

# Flag them so any downstream comparison can be repeated without them
meta["prep_suspect"] = meta.index.isin(row_h)

Row-H wells kept: 7 | precursors deviating by > 0.5 log2: 8.9% | deviation vs RT: Spearman rho = +0.01
Serum precursor CV: 10.4% with row H, 9.7% without

Interpretation

  • Drift is gone. Run-level signal is flat across the sequence for all three groups, and the step near injection 200 has disappeared.
  • The PCA is organised by biology only: PC1 is plasma vs serum, and injection order no longer organises any axis.
  • Plate-3 row H is only partly rescued.
    • The intensity offset is fixed (−0.41 → about 0 log2), so part of the problem behaved like a loading difference.
    • Their correlation to the serum profile stays lower (about 0.988 vs 0.998), and about 9% of their precursors still deviate by more than 0.5 log2, unrelated to retention time.
    • That is a composition-level difference, consistent with a digestion or recovery difference on that row, and normalization cannot fix it.
    • Dropping the 7 remaining wells would lower serum CV by about 0.7 points.
  • Decision: the pre-registered rule stands: 4 runs excluded, these 7 kept. They are flagged prep_suspect in the exported sample table, so any downstream comparison can be re-run without them as a sensitivity check. Tightening the rule now would be fitting thresholds to the data.

6. Protein roll-up¶

Notebook 01 (§11) showed the report's PG.Quantity cannot be reconstructed from the filtered precursors, and that serum fibrinogen-A was oddly bimodal. So proteins are rebuilt here from the normalized precursors.

Method How Known weakness
Top-3 sum Sum of the 3 most intense precursors A missing precursor lowers the sum even if the protein did not change
Median polish Robust additive model: overall + precursor effect + run effect Needs several precursors per run to be stable
MaxLFQ Pairwise median ratios between runs, then least squares (Cox et al. 2014) Depends on precursors shared between pairs of runs

First, a check that the implementations work, on synthetic data where the true protein levels are known.

In [12]:
# Synthetic test: 8 precursors x 12 runs, known protein levels, 30% of values missing at random
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
true_level = rng.normal(20, 1, 12)                         # protein level per run
response = rng.normal(0, 2, 8)                             # each precursor ionises differently
sim = true_level[None, :] + response[:, None] + rng.normal(0, 0.05, (8, 12))
sim[rng.random(sim.shape) < 0.3] = np.nan
sim = pd.DataFrame(sim)

rows = []
for name, fn in [("top-3 sum", rollup.top_n_sum), ("median polish", rollup.median_polish), ("MaxLFQ", rollup.maxlfq)]:
    est = fn(sim)
    ok = ~np.isnan(est)
    # Only RELATIVE levels are identifiable, so compare after centring both
    err = (est[ok] - est[ok].mean()) - (true_level[ok] - true_level[ok].mean())
    rows.append({"method": name, "runs recovered": f"{ok.sum()}/12", "RMS error (log2)": np.sqrt(np.mean(err ** 2))})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("method").round(3)
Out[12]:
runs recovered RMS error (log2)
method
top-3 sum 12/12 0.72
median polish 12/12 0.03
MaxLFQ 12/12 0.02

Result: MaxLFQ and median polish recover the true relative levels to within the simulated measurement noise (0.05 log2). The top-3 sum is off by about 0.7 log2, purely because of missing values. With the implementations validated, they are compared on the real data.

In [13]:
# Roll up the normalized precursors with each method, and score at protein level
protein_of = annot["Protein.Group"]
rollups = {
    "DIA-NN PG.Normalised (as delivered)": np.log2(qc.to_matrix(precursors, "PG.Normalised", "Protein.Group")[runs]),
    "top-3 sum": rollup.rollup(normalized, protein_of, rollup.top_n_sum),
    "median polish": rollup.rollup(normalized, protein_of, rollup.median_polish),
    "MaxLFQ, >=1 shared precursor": rollup.rollup(normalized, protein_of, rollup.maxlfq, min_ratio_count=1),
    "MaxLFQ, >=2 shared precursors": rollup.rollup(normalized, protein_of, rollup.maxlfq, min_ratio_count=2),
}

pg_gene = annot.drop_duplicates("Protein.Group").set_index("Protein.Group")["Genes"]
plasma_runs = meta.index[meta["sample_type"] == "Plasma"]

def protein_score(m):
    out = {"protein groups": int(m.notna().any(axis=1).sum()),
           "median proteins / run": int(m.notna().sum().median())}
    for g, cols in [("QC", qc_runs), ("Plasma", plasma_runs), ("Serum", serum_runs)]:
        out[f"CV % {g}"] = qc.cv_percent(2 ** m[cols], 0.7).median()
    for gene in ["FGA", "FGB", "FGG"]:
        pg = pg_gene.index[pg_gene == gene][0]
        v = m.loc[pg] if pg in m.index else pd.Series(np.nan, index=runs)
        out[f"{gene} serum runs quantified"] = int(v[serum_runs].notna().sum())
        out[f"{gene} log2 P/S"] = v[plasma_runs].median() - v[serum_runs].median()
    fga = m.loc[pg_gene.index[pg_gene == "FGA"][0], serum_runs].dropna()
    out["FGA SD in serum"] = fga.std()
    return out

rollup_board = pd.DataFrame({k: protein_score(v) for k, v in rollups.items()}).T
rollup_board.round(2)

FGG: 39 precursors; quantified in >= 10 serum runs: 1
That precursor: DTVQIHDITGKDC(UniMod:4)QDIANK3 | plasma median log2 5.2 vs median of all FGG precursors 8.9

Interpretation

  • DIA-NN's protein values look precise (CVs about 7%) but carry the serum FGA bimodality (SD 0.85 log2) found in Notebook 01.
  • Top-3 summing inflates fold changes and loses proteins, because missing top precursors drag the sum down. That matches the synthetic test.
  • MaxLFQ gives the lowest CVs (about 4%) and resolves the FGA bimodality (SD 0.85 → 0.17 log2), confirming that the bimodality was a property of DIA-NN's protein quantity, not of the sample.
  • But MaxLFQ that accepts single shared precursors reports FGG as nearly equal in plasma and serum (log2 P/S about 0.6), which is biologically impossible: clotting removes fibrinogen. The figure shows why:
    • in serum, FGG is detected essentially through one precursor, and it is one of FGG's weakest even in plasma, near the noise floor
    • a ratio built on that single near-noise precursor is compressed towards 1
    • so the method reports "equal" where the truth is "absent"
  • Requiring at least 2 shared precursors, the default in the original MaxLFQ paper, turns FGG in serum into "not reliably quantified" (1 of 79 runs), which is the honest answer.
    • The cost: 26 protein groups seen only through a single precursor drop out of the protein table (184 → 158).
    • They remain available at precursor level.

Decision: MaxLFQ with ≥ 2 shared precursors.

  • It is the most precise roll-up, and it was validated on synthetic data.
  • It refuses to report a protein that rests on one precursor.
  • A lesson worth stating in an interview: the lowest CV is not the deciding criterion. A method that turns absence into equality looks precise and is wrong.

7. Is the biology still there after the full pipeline?¶

Same positive control as Notebook 01, now on the final protein values:

  • Fibrinogen should be much higher in plasma than in serum.
  • Proteins not involved in clotting should be flat.
  • Platelet-released proteins (PF4, PPBP), which would test the opposite direction (higher in serum), are not detected at this depth on a 5-minute gradient, so the control is one-directional.

    • Their "plasma/serum" medians come from the handful of serum runs where something was detected, so they are not fold changes.
    • Their correct description is "present in plasma, below reliable quantification in serum."

  • The flat controls stay flat (within about ±0.2 log2). The pipeline has not invented differences.

8. Sensitivity: do the conclusions depend on the protein-group filter?¶

Notebook 01 chose protein-group rule D and promised to re-check under:

  • rule B (PG q ≤ 1% per run, stricter run by run)
  • rule E (PG q ≤ 1% in ≥ 50% of a matrix's runs, stricter overall)

The full chosen pipeline (M3 → sample-anchored drift → MaxLFQ with ≥ 2 shared precursors) is re-run from the report under each rule.

In [16]:
# Rebuild the precursor table under each protein-group rule, from the cached full report
report = diann_io.load_diann_report(ROOT / "data" / "raw" / "data.diannoutput.qc.tsv", cache_dir=PROCESSED)
report = report[report["run"].astype(str).isin(runs)]
meta_all = metadata.parse_run_names(report["run"])
support = qc.protein_group_support(report, meta_all, q=0.01)

rules = {
    "B  PG q <= 1% per run": report["PG.Q.Value"] <= 0.01,
    "D  >= 25% of a matrix (chosen)": report["Protein.Group"].isin(support.index[(support >= 0.25).any(axis=1)]),
    "E  >= 50% of a matrix": report["Protein.Group"].isin(support.index[(support >= 0.50).any(axis=1)]),
}
sens_rows = []
for name, keep in rules.items():
    sub = report[keep]
    m_raw = np.log2(qc.to_matrix(sub, "Precursor.Quantity"))
    kept_runs = [r for r in runs if r in m_raw.columns]      # a strict rule can empty whole runs
    m_raw = m_raw[kept_runs]
    m_rt = sub.groupby("Precursor.Id")["RT"].median()
    m_norm = normalize.rt_lowess_normalize(m_raw, m_rt, frac=0.3)
    m_norm, _ = normalize.sample_drift_correction(m_norm, injection, groups, frac=m7_frac)
    m_prot = rollup.rollup(m_norm, sub.drop_duplicates("Precursor.Id").set_index("Precursor.Id")["Protein.Group"],
                           rollup.maxlfq, min_ratio_count=2)
    s = protein_score(m_prot.reindex(columns=runs))
    sens_rows.append({"rule": name, "runs with data": len(kept_runs), "precursors": m_raw.shape[0], **{k: s[k] for k in
                      ["protein groups", "median proteins / run", "CV % Plasma", "CV % Serum", "CV % QC", "FGA log2 P/S"]}})
pd.DataFrame(sens_rows).set_index("rule").round(2)
Out[16]:
runs with data precursors protein groups median proteins / run CV % Plasma CV % Serum CV % QC FGA log2 P/S
rule
B  PG q <= 1% per run 164 3882 198 118 2.34 2.68 1.61 5.85
D  >= 25% of a matrix (chosen) 205 3674 158 152 3.73 3.96 2.37 5.76
E  >= 50% of a matrix 205 3518 132 128 3.13 3.51 1.91 5.76

Interpretation

  • Rule B is not viable for this experiment: it empties 41 of the 205 runs entirely.
    • With about 180 protein groups per run, the smallest q-value a run can produce is about 1/180 ≈ 0.006.
    • In 42 of the 209 runs, even the best protein's q exceeds 0.01, so a per-run 1% protein FDR is at the resolution limit of this experiment.
    • This also corrects Notebook 01, whose comparison reported rule B's median over the surviving runs only.
  • Stricter rules give lower CVs because they keep fewer, more abundant proteins (rule E: 132 groups, CV 3.1–3.5%; rule D: 158 groups, CV 3.7–4.0%). That changes which proteins are measured, not how well the pipeline measures them.
  • The biological conclusion does not move: fibrinogen-A is 5.76–5.85 log2 higher in plasma under every rule.
  • Rule D stands. It keeps every run and more proteins, at a modest precision cost that comes from including lower-abundance proteins.

9. Missing values: why imputation is deferred to Notebook 03¶

In [17]:

      f"{proteins.isna().mean().mean():.1%} of values missing")

Protein groups quantified in every run: 128 (81%)
Out[17]:
mean_log2_intensity fraction_missing n_features
intensity_decile
1 8.47 1.01e-01 32
2 9.76 6.20e-02 31

4 12.59 6.29e-03 31
5 14.66 3.25e-02 32

Interpretation and decision

  • Missingness at protein level is low: 4.1% of values are missing, and 81% of protein groups are quantified in every run. It is concentrated in the least abundant proteins, plus matrix-specific absences (FGB and FGG in serum account for most of the missing values among abundant proteins).
  • In this dataset, imputation would change no conclusion. The samples are technical replicates and the one real difference (fibrinogen) is unambiguous.
  • The choice of imputation method can only be graded where true fold changes are known. Notebook 03 uses the hybrid-proteome benchmark (PXD028735), where it can be measured how each approach (no imputation, low-value imputation, model-based handling) biases fold changes and false-discovery rates.
  • So the protein matrix is exported without imputation, and missing values stay explicit.

long_norm.to_parquet(PROCESSED / "02_precursors_normalized.parquet", index=False)

      f"protein matrix and the sample table to {PROCESSED.relative_to(ROOT)}/")

Saved 753,170 normalized precursor values, a 158 x 205 protein matrix and the sample table to data/processed/
Question Finding Decision
Is a global scale factor enough? No: a component still tracks injection order almost perfectly (|ρ| = 0.96) Rejected
RT-dependent normalization? Sample CV 24% → 11.5%; reproduces DIA-NN's method (r = 0.9998); leaves a precursor-specific drift component (|ρ| = 0.94, ~5% of variance) Kept as step 1
QC-anchored correction (authors' linear, or our LOWESS)? Best QC precision, worse sample precision. The QC drifts ~1.2× faster than serum, so samples are over-corrected; 18% of precursors have no QC anchor Rejected for correction; QC kept for monitoring
Sample-anchored per-precursor drift (M7)? Lowest cross-fitted sample CVs (10.7–10.9%); the only method leaving no PC tied to run order (max |ρ| = 0.09). Valid because run order is randomized Chosen: M3 → M7. Not to be used in non-randomized designs
How low can sample CVs go? ~6.5% injection noise + ~8.5–9% preparation noise ≈ 10.8%. Preparation noise cannot be normalized away The precision floor, now explained
Plate-3 row H? Offset fixed; a composition difference remains (r 0.988 vs 0.998; 9% of precursors deviate > 0.5 log2) Pre-registered rule stands; 7 wells flagged prep_suspect
Protein roll-up? MaxLFQ is most precise and fixes the FGA bimodality. With single-precursor ratios it reports absent FGG as "equal". MaxLFQ, ≥ 2 shared precursors (validated on synthetic truth); 158 protein groups
Biology preserved? FGA 5.8 log2 higher in plasma; FGB and FGG absent in serum; non-clotting proteins flat (within ±0.2) Pass
Robust to the protein-group rule? The fibrinogen difference is stable. Rule B empties 41 runs (per-run protein q is at its resolution limit) Rule D confirmed
Imputation? 4% missing; cannot be graded without known truth Deferred to Notebook 03 (benchmark)

Limitations

  • RT-dependent normalization assumes most precursors are unchanged in each run. Sample-anchored drift correction assumes randomized run order. Both hold here, but both must be re-checked for any new design, especially perturbation experiments where many proteins move, such as a degrader screen.
  • The variance decomposition adds CVs in quadrature, which is an approximation.
  • The explanation for the QC drifting faster than samples (vial ageing) is plausible but not tested.
